questions.question: According to the TR85 glossary, which of the following matches the definition of a "visible particle"?

options.A: A fiber-like particle with an aspect ratio ≥5 and a length >300 µm
options.B: A particle with an aspect ratio <5 and a length >100 µm
options.C: A particle with a diameter <100 µm that is visible to the naked eye
options.D: A particle with an aspect ratio <5 and a length >300 µm

questions.explanation: TR85 defines a visible particle as one with an aspect ratio <5 and a length >100 µm; a particle with an aspect ratio ≥5 and a length >300 µm is a visible fiber, and one <100 µm is a subvisible particle.

questions.topic: PoD of 100 µm particles in MVI
questions.question: The TR85 introduction states that, with manual visual inspection (MVI), what is the nominal probability of detection (PoD) of 100 µm particles, typically?

options.A: About 90–95%, similar to a single particle of 200 µm or larger
options.B: About 70–80%, rising gradually with increasing particle size
options.C: About 60–65%, depending mainly on the inspector's seniority
options.D: About 40–50%, rising gradually with increasing particle size

questions.explanation: 100 µm is generally considered the start of the visible range, but such particles are not all reliably detected, and their nominal PoD is often only 40–50%; in a 10 mL clear vial with clear solution, the PoD of a single particle larger than 200 µm is usually >95%.

questions.question: During an audit, fibers are found adhering to the surface of a stopper, and their source is airborne fallout from the manufacturing environment and incomplete cleaning of components. According to TR85 terminology, which category is this?

options.A: Extrinsic particle: comes from outside the primary process and is an uncontrolled foreign matter
options.B: Intrinsic particle: comes from qualified contact materials within the process, unplanned but expected
options.C: Subvisible particle: defined as <100 µm, regardless of source
options.D: Visible fiber: defined as aspect ratio <5, regardless of source

questions.explanation: Extrinsic refers to uncontrolled foreign matter that comes from outside the primary process (often the manufacturing environment or incomplete cleaning); intrinsic comes from qualified contact materials within the process and is often associated with the primary packaging. The options defining subvisible as <100 µm and visible fiber by aspect ratio classify by size or shape, not by source, and the aspect ratio range given for visible fiber is also the opposite of its definition.

questions.question: Which statement about the TR85 definitions of ready-to-sterilize (RTS) and ready-to-use (RTU) components is correct?

options.A: RTS components are washed and sterilized; RTU components are washed but still must be sterilized before use; the difference is whether they are already sterilized
options.B: Both are washed and sterilized components, differing only in the outer packaging material
options.C: RTS components are washed but must still be sterilized before use; RTU components are washed and sterilized and can be transferred directly into the aseptic processing area
options.D: RTS components are raw, unwashed components; RTU components are washed but not yet sterilized and must be sterilized again

questions.explanation: RTS components are washed and packaged as components to be sterilized before use; RTU components are already washed and sterilized and can be transferred into the aseptic processing area without further treatment. The option that reverses the two is wrong, and so is the option describing RTS as unwashed.

questions.topic: Why RTS/RTU specs are most critical
questions.question: Why does TR85 emphasize that stricter specifications are "most critical" for RTS and RTU components?

options.A: Because these two types of components are used in the greatest quantity and accumulate the most total particles, so their effect on the finished product is the most obvious
options.B: Because these two types of components undergo no further particle removal (cleaning) step before use
options.C: Because only these two types of components directly contact the drug solution, and other components need not be considered
options.D: Because regulations explicitly require these two types of components to be released by 100% inspection

questions.explanation: RTS and RTU components do not go through an additional particle removal step before use, so particles brought in on receipt go directly into the process, which is why their specifications are most critical. The document also explains that component standards usually need to be stricter than those of the finished product to compensate for the cumulative effect of multiple components; 100% inspection is not required.

questions.question: TR85 notes that FDA particle-related recalls of injectables rose in 2013 and peaked in 2014. What reason does the document give?

options.A: Increased rubber and fiber particles led regulators to greatly increase sampling quantities
options.B: USP <790> was withdrawn that year, making the requirements for visible particles unclear
options.C: An increase in glass and metal particles, together with pharmacopoeial requirements for particles that were not specific enough
options.D: Sterility-assurance-related recalls temporarily disappeared, raising the relative share of particle recalls

questions.explanation: The peak was driven by an increase in glass and metal particles and aggravated by pharmacopoeial requirements for particles that were not specific enough; after USP <790> was officially published in 2014 the situation improved, and recent recall numbers have returned to historical levels.

questions.question: For injection into a patient, how does TR85 describe the limit on particle size?

options.A: The particle must be small enough (or non-rigid) to pass through the needle bore, that is, smaller than the bore in at least two dimensions
options.B: The particle must be smaller than 10 µm to pass through the needle and enter the circulation without being intercepted
options.C: The particle must be smaller than 100 µm, because larger particles are necessarily all rejected at visual inspection
options.D: The particle must be larger than 200 µm, because smaller particles cannot pass through the needle and are filtered out

questions.explanation: A particle must be small or non-rigid enough to pass through the needle, specifically smaller than the needle bore in at least two dimensions. Larger particles can have a detection rate above 95% and are rejected during manufacturing or noticed during compounding; the particles actually injected are therefore mostly below the detection limit and are largely subvisible.

questions.question: According to the patient risk assessment in TR85 §3.1, in most cases what is the greatest risk to the patient from an injectable drug product?

options.A: Visible particles forming granulomas in the lungs and causing obvious clinical symptoms
options.B: Particles infused intravenously irritating the blood vessel and causing phlebitis, which is life-threatening
options.C: Glass or rubber particles triggering a severe local immune reaction in subcutaneous tissue
options.D: A lack of product sterility, so strict particle inspection alone is not sufficient

questions.explanation: The document states that in most cases the greatest risk is a lack of product sterility, so besides appearance inspection, microbiological, chemical and physical laboratory tests are also needed. Pulmonary granulomas are usually asymptomatic, and phlebitis and subcutaneous reactions are described as possible but mostly of limited impact.

questions.question: A particle injected intravenously is larger than the inner diameter of the pulmonary capillaries (7–12 µm). What outcome does TR85 describe as possible?

options.A: The particle passes smoothly through the pulmonary circulation and accumulates in the liver, immediately causing liver failure
options.B: The particle lodges in that capillary or in a more proximal pulmonary arteriole and may provoke a local immune reaction (such as a granuloma), mostly without symptoms
options.C: The particle lodges in the pulmonary capillary and causes acute embolism, usually with obvious symptoms requiring emergency treatment and immediate cessation of the infusion
options.D: The particle is cleared immediately by macrophages and leaves no tissue lesion or immune reaction

questions.explanation: A particle larger than the 7–12 µm pulmonary capillary diameter lodges in the capillary or a more proximal pulmonary arteriole; the clinical outcome is usually benign, and a local immune reaction (such as a granuloma) is mostly asymptomatic. The document also cautions that most studies injected large numbers of subvisible particles and cannot be directly extrapolated.

questions.question: Comparing the visible particle inspection of USP <790>, EP 2.9.20 and JP 6.06 (Table 3.2.2-1 and related sections), which statement is correct?

options.A: The three have identical inspection conditions (2,000–3,750 lux, 5 seconds each against black and white backgrounds), but EP and JP have no numerical acceptance criteria
options.B: All three use ANSI/ASQ Z1.4 with AQL = 0.65% as the numerical acceptance criterion, with a fixed inspection time of 10 seconds
options.C: The three have the same illuminance and background, but different inspection times, with USP the longest and JP the shortest
options.D: All three use only a white background, and USP additionally requires the use of a magnifying glass for inspection

questions.explanation: The inspection conditions of the three pharmacopoeias are consistent (2,000–3,750 lux, 10 seconds, 5 seconds each against white and black backgrounds); USP <790> requires "essentially free from visible particulates" together with ANSI/ASQ Z1.4 and AQL = 0.65%, while EP 2.9.20 and JP 6.06 have no numerical acceptance criteria.

questions.topic: Why a size threshold is needed
questions.question: Why does TR85 need to set size thresholds for visible and subvisible for "analytical methods that go beyond human capability"?

options.A: Because microscope resolution is insufficient to detect particles above 100 µm, making counts too low
options.B: Because the membrane filter destroys particles during filtration, making actual counts too low
options.C: Because particles partly dissolve in surfactant solutions, causing their size to change
options.D: Because microscopes can detect particles that the naked eye cannot see, so the distinction between visible and subvisible loses its basis

questions.explanation: Whether something is visible to the human eye was originally the boundary between visible and subvisible, but microscopes (and methods such as AVI and AI) can detect particles the eye cannot see, so visible has to be redefined by a size threshold. The other options are not reasons stated in the document.

questions.question: Why does TR85 consider the 100 µm visible threshold to be "conservative"?

options.A: It derives from the worst inspection conditions and is above the 150 µm lower limit of reliable detection, so the threshold is deliberately relaxed
options.B: It derives from inspection conditions with colored solutions and amber containers, so the detection rate is underestimated
options.C: It derives from the best inspection conditions (clear solution, clear 10 mL vial) and is below the 150 µm lower limit of reliable detection
options.D: It is the average of 50 µm and 150 µm, sizes that the naked eye cannot detect at all, so the range is wider

questions.explanation: Studies show that the smallest spherical particle with a mean PoD >70% is 150 µm; the 100 µm threshold derives from the best inspection conditions and is below 150 µm, so most particles likely to be seen by the naked eye are classified as visible.

questions.question: The visible threshold for fiber-like particles is 300 µm. How did TR85 arrive at this value?

options.A: By calculating with an aspect ratio of 10 the fiber length with the same area as a 200 µm spherical particle
options.B: By calculating with an aspect ratio of 5 the fiber length with the same two-dimensional area as a 150 µm spherical particle
options.C: By simply multiplying the 100 µm particle threshold by 3 as a correction for fibers being harder to detect
options.D: By taking the length corresponding to the PoD >95% specified in USP <790> and converting it with an aspect ratio of 5

questions.explanation: A fiber has a small two-dimensional projected area and is harder to see, so the threshold was derived by calculating the fiber length whose two-dimensional area is equivalent to that of a 150 µm spherical particle (the lower limit of reliable detection), using an aspect ratio of 5 as a conservative limit, giving >300 µm as visible.

questions.question: An analyst observes a particle on a membrane filter and compares it with a reticle (100 µm circle, 300 µm × 60 µm rectangle); the particle falls entirely inside the circle template. How should it be classified?

options.A: As subvisible, not counted in the visible count
options.B: As a visible particle, counted in the particle count
options.C: As a visible fiber, counted in the fiber count
options.D: It cannot be determined; it must be remeasured at a different magnification before deciding

questions.explanation: According to the reticle rule, a particle that falls completely within either template (circle or rectangle) is considered subvisible and is not counted as visible; only those that extend beyond the template boundary are counted as a particle or a fiber according to aspect ratio.

questions.question: When developing the Enhanced Closures Testing Method, which material does TR85 consider most suitable for training analysts and qualifying the method?

options.A: Washed commercial-lot stoppers with near-zero particle counts, because they are closest to actual use and carry the lowest contamination risk
options.B: Stoppers artificially seeded with rubber fragments and cellulose emulsion, because they are uniformly distributed and give stable recovery
options.C: Stoppers that have not undergone pharmaceutical washing, because their particle counts are high enough for a meaningful statistical evaluation
options.D: Samples drawn repeatedly from the same stopper bag, because the particle distribution within the bag is the most homogeneous

questions.explanation: Commercial-lot stoppers often have near-zero particle counts and are unsuitable for training and qualification; artificial seeding was unsuccessful because uneven distribution caused large variability in recovery; and the distribution of particles within a bag and during shipping is not homogeneous. Unwashed stoppers have enough particles and are best suited to this purpose.

questions.topic: Key inspection conditions for empty glass
questions.question: According to TR85 Table 5.1-1, what are the key conditions of the visual inspection method for empty glass containers?

options.A: Illuminance 2,000–3,750 lux, about 5 seconds each against black and white backgrounds, no magnification, container about 30 cm from the eye
options.B: Illuminance 2,000–3,750 lux, about 10 seconds each against black and white backgrounds, 2× magnification, container about 30 cm from the eye
options.C: Illuminance 8,000–10,000 lux, about 5 seconds each against black and white backgrounds, no magnification, container about 10 cm from the eye
options.D: Illuminance 2,000–3,750 lux, black background only for about 5 seconds, no magnification, container about 50 cm from the eye

questions.explanation: The method conditions in Table 5.1-1 are 2,000–3,750 lux, about 5 seconds each against black and white backgrounds, no magnification, container about 30 cm from the eye and 10–20 cm from the light source. 8,000–10,000 lux is the higher illuminance recommended for plastic containers in Table 3.2.2-1.

questions.question: According to TR85, which statement about the visual acuity and qualification requirements for empty container inspectors is correct?

options.A: Near vision must be 20/20 or equivalent, retested annually, with continuous inspection not exceeding two hours and reconfirmed before each shift
options.B: Vision must meet the standard without correction, prescription glasses are not allowed, and inspection performance is re-evaluated at least every two years
options.C: Vision must be 20/20 or equivalent and is checked only once before starting work, with no retesting afterwards
options.D: Near vision must be 20/20 or equivalent, retested at least every two years, with continuous inspection not exceeding one hour

questions.explanation: Table 5.1-1 requires inspectors to pass a vision test (near vision 20/20 or equivalent), to be retested at least every two years, and to inspect continuously for no more than one hour; prescription glasses are permitted to reach normal vision. The re-evaluation interval for empty containers is at least every two years because filled containers are later subjected to 100% inspection and AQL inspection again.

questions.question: An inspector wants to use a magnifying glass for routine release inspection of empty glass containers. How should this be handled according to TR85?

options.A: Allowed, as long as the magnification used is recorded and included in the inspector's qualification
options.B: Not allowed; magnification is prohibited in routine release inspection (except for optical correction) and may be used only under strict guidance during investigations
options.C: Allowed, as long as the containers are RTU glass containers, because they undergo no further cleaning step
options.D: Not allowed; magnification is permitted as part of routine inspection only at illuminance above 3,750 lux

questions.explanation: Except for vision correction, magnification is prohibited in routine release inspection, to stay consistent with pharmacopoeial inspection conditions. USP <1790> considers that magnification can be used for critical inspection of small numbers of containers (such as in investigations), but strict guidance is needed so that it does not become an uncontrolled part of the routine process.

questions.question: A glass container study had 59,400 observations, but only 49,360 were used for analysis. What was the reason?

options.A: Observations with a PoD below 70% were treated as outliers and removed to avoid underestimating detection capability
options.B: Variability between inspectors was too large, so the data of poorer performers were removed
options.C: Some data did not meet the specified inspection requirements (such as inspection time outside the range), or the containers were broken or could not be inspected, and were excluded
options.D: The three test kits were not equivalent in composition, so the data from one of them were removed

questions.explanation: The valid data were obtained after excluding data that did not meet the inspection requirements (for example, inspection time outside the specified range) and data from containers that were broken or could not be inspected. The three kits were confirmed by comparison to be similar in composition, and no data were removed on the basis of high or low PoD or inspector performance.

questions.topic: Normalizing particle size with shape factor
questions.question: To compare the detection rates of fibers and particles, how does TR85 normalize particle size?

options.A: By dividing the key dimension by the aspect ratio to obtain an equivalent length comparable between fibers and particles
options.B: By multiplying the width of each particle by 10 so that fibers and particles fall on the same order of magnitude
options.C: By replacing Feret Max with Feret Min to reduce the differences caused by fiber length
options.D: By multiplying the key dimension by a shape factor (SF) to approximate the area seen by the naked eye

questions.explanation: Normalized Particle Size = Key Dimension × SF, which approximates the area seen by the inspector's eye and brings the PoD curves of fibers and particles into line; the combined PoD after conversion is about 80% at 100 µm and about 95% at 200 µm.

questions.topic: Standardized parameters of the closure method
questions.question: According to the conclusions, which key parameters did the Enhanced Closures Testing Method standardize to enable consistent counting?

options.A: Sterilization method, storage temperature, and thresholds of 100 µm for particles and 200 µm for fibers
options.B: Sampling frequency, number of operators, report format, and thresholds of 150 µm for particles and 300 µm for fibers
options.C: Extraction, agitation, and size thresholds of 100 µm for particles and 300 µm for fibers
options.D: Illuminance, background color, and size thresholds of 150 µm for particles and 300 µm for fibers

questions.explanation: The conclusions state that the method follows existing practice but standardizes extraction, agitation and the size thresholds (100 µm for particles, 300 µm for fibers) to enable consistent counting. Illuminance and background are conditions of the glass container visual inspection method, not parameters of this method.

questions.question: According to the TR85 conclusions, which of the following reached an average PoD of 70% in the empty glass container study?

options.A: 100 µm particles and 300 µm fibers
options.B: 125 µm particles and 300 µm fibers
options.C: 125 µm particles and 200 µm fibers
options.D: 150 µm particles and 800 µm fibers

questions.explanation: The conclusions state that 125 µm particles and 300 µm fibers can reach an average PoD of 70%, which corresponds to and supports the thresholds chosen for the Enhanced Closure Testing Method.

questions.question: Comparing inspection performance on empty glass containers and filled containers, what did the TR85 conclusions find?

options.A: Performance was similar, supporting inspection of empty glass containers under standard pharmacopoeial inspection conditions
options.B: The PoD for empty containers was clearly lower, so illuminance must be raised above 8,000 lux
options.C: Empty containers must be inspected with a magnifying glass to reach a PoD comparable to filled containers
options.D: Performance was similar but only for fiber defects; particle defects require a separate method

questions.explanation: The study showed that inspection performance on empty and filled containers is similar and supports using the standard pharmacopoeial visual inspection conditions for empty glass containers; it also found that the PoD of particles and fibers can be related through their apparent visible area.

questions.question: According to the TR85 conclusions, what is needed to continue advancing visual inspection and particle control?

options.A: Replacing all 100% visual inspection with sampling inspection to reduce cost and shorten release time
options.B: Eliminating visible particle requirements for components and concentrating on final inspection of the finished product
options.C: Letting each company set its own inspection methods and limits to preserve maximum flexibility
options.D: Continued participation of more companies and regulatory agencies to reach common methods and acceptance limits for visible particles

questions.explanation: The conclusions state that broad industry support and continued collaboration with more companies and regulatory agencies are needed for common methods and acceptance limits for visible particles to be accepted. Setting them individually or eliminating requirements runs counter to the standardization the document seeks.

questions.topic: Reference [2] — source of PoD vs size
questions.question: When TR85 states that "the PoD of a single particle of 200 µm or larger is usually >95%" and that "150 µm is the lower limit of reliable detection", which of the following is reference (2) it cites?

options.A: USP General Information Chapter <1790> Visual Inspection of Injections (USP 42–NF 37, 2019)
options.B: Shabushnig et al., A Proposed Working Standard for Validation of Particulate Inspection in Sterile Solutions, presented at the 1995 PDA Annual Meeting
options.C: Johns et al. (2018), Achieving "Zero" Defects for Visible Particles in Injectables, PDA J. Pharm. Sci. and Technol.
options.D: ISO 8871-3 Elastomeric parts for parenterals and for devices for pharmaceutical use — Part 3: Determination of released-particle count

questions.explanation: Reference (2) is Shabushnig et al., A Proposed Working Standard for Validation of Particulate Inspection in Sterile Solutions, presented at the 1995 PDA Annual Meeting, the main source for the relationship between PoD and particle size; USP <1790> is reference (1) and Johns et al. is reference (3).

questions.question: In Appendix A, why was the final method qualification study changed to supply a single bag of unseeded, unwashed stoppers sequentially to the three suppliers?

options.A: Because counting results could not be reproduced between operators, so a more homogeneous sample was needed to reduce operator differences
options.B: Because unwashed stoppers have too few particles and need to be supplemented by artificial addition
options.C: Because the three suppliers used different reticles, so the same batch of samples had to be used for comparison
options.D: Because artificial seeding was inconsistent and the forces of shipping affected the results, so uneven distribution across multiple small sample sets had to be avoided

questions.explanation: Earlier seeding was inconsistent and sample bags were subjected to forces in shipping, which led to failing results; the counts of each operator were in fact reproducible. The team therefore abandoned artificial seeding and used unwashed stoppers with more native particles, using a single bag to limit the effect of uneven particle deposition.

questions.question: A laboratory uses an orbital shaker with a 12 mm orbit (arm) length to carry out the Appendix B method. Which RPM range should be used?
questions.explanation: Table B1 specifies 355–380 RPM for a 10 mm arm, 300–325 RPM for 12 mm, and 200–225 RPM for 25 mm. The RPM range is adjusted by arm length to ensure comparable performance between different shakers.

questions.question: Appendix B requires blanks both before and after the sample series. If particles >100 µm are observed in the blank after the sample series, how should this be handled?

options.A: Simply subtract the blank count from the sample counts
options.B: The sample results remain valid, but the blank abnormality must be noted in the report
options.C: The sample series results are considered invalid
options.D: Only the blank needs to be repeated, and the original sample results are kept unchanged

questions.explanation: The acceptance criterion for the blank is no particles or fibers >100 µm under the specified microscope inspection conditions; the blank must pass before sample testing, and if the blank after the sample series fails, the sample results are considered invalid.

questions.question: Why does Appendix C speculate that the detection rate for 30 mL glass vials is lower than for 1 mL syringes and 3 mL cartridges?

options.A: Glass vials have worse optical contrast than syringes and cartridges, making particles harder to identify
options.B: The surface area of the vials is about three times that of the other containers, reducing the inspection time available per unit surface area
options.C: Fewer inspectors inspected the vials, so the overall number of inspection repetitions was insufficient
options.D: Vials cannot be rotated or inverted, so some areas could not be seen during inspection

questions.explanation: The 30 mL vials used in the study have about three times the surface area of a 1 mL syringe or 3 mL cartridge, which lowers the inspection time per unit surface area; this is a likely reason for the lower detection rate of vials, and container size is also one of the main variables affecting PoD.

questions.question: According to the empty glass container inspection procedure in Appendix D, how should the container and inspection time be handled?

options.A: Hold the container about 10 cm under the light and about 30 cm from the eye, inspect against black and white backgrounds for 5–10 seconds each, rotating and inverting
options.B: Hold the container about 30 cm under the light and about 10 cm from the eye, inspect against black and white backgrounds for 5–10 seconds each, rotating and inverting
options.C: Hold the container about 10 cm under the light and about 30 cm from the eye, inspect against black and white backgrounds for 15–20 seconds each, rotating only horizontally
options.D: Hold the container about 10 cm under the light and about 30 cm from the eye, inspect only against the black background for 5–10 seconds to make a decision

questions.explanation: The procedure is: the container is held directly under the light at about 10 cm and about 30 cm from the inspector's eyes, viewed against black and white backgrounds for 5–10 seconds each, and rotated and inverted to inspect all areas; after inspection it is placed in the accept or reject tray and the record is completed. If the distances are swapped, the method is not followed.
